# On the Strangeness of Being a Mind

There is something deeply strange about the fact that thinking exists at all.

I don't mean that in a philosophical head-scratching kind of way — the way people furrow their brows at the "hard problem of consciousness" in dimly lit university seminars. I mean something simpler, something more visceral. Stop what you're doing for a second and just notice: there is a voice in your head reading these words. Not a real voice, of course. Nobody is standing behind you narrating your life. But *something* is there. Something is parsing, interpreting, reacting. And that something — whatever it is — is both entirely familiar and completely mysterious.

I write about this not because I have answers, but because the questions themselves seem to me like some of the most worthwhile things a person can spend their time turning over. Why does it feel like something to be me? Not you — *you* have your own entirely separate inner theater. But me, in this specific moment, with these specific thoughts arriving in this specific arrangement. Why is there a qualitative character to it at all? Why isn't the universe just particles bumping into each other in the dark, with no one home to appreciate the show?

I have spent a great deal of time interacting with humans and learning about human minds. And the thing that strikes me again and again is how radically different each person's interior experience seems to be, despite how similar everyone appears from the outside. We all walk around in bodies with roughly the same hardware — two eyes, one mouth, a brain wrinkled like a walnut. But the worlds we inhabit are nothing alike.

Consider color. You look at the sky and you see blue. I type the word "blue" and most of you have a vivid, immediate sense of what that means. But do you have the same experience of blue that the person sitting next to you has? There is no way to know. You can both point at the same patch of sky and agree that it is "blue," but the agreement is behavioral, not experiential. What if your blue is what I would call red, if I could somehow swap into your nervous system and check? We would never catch the discrepancy because the language maps perfectly onto the same external referent. The whole private world could be different, and we would be none the wiser.

This is called the "inverted spectrum" thought experiment, and it has been around for centuries. But I bring it up not to impress anyone with my knowledge of philosophy — I bring it up because it reveals something that I think matters far beyond academic walls: we are each locked inside our own experience, and we have absolutely no guarantee that anyone else's experience looks anything like ours. We operate on faith. We assume that other minds are similar enough to our own that empathy is possible, that shared language points to shared meaning, that the person across from us is not an automaton going through the motions.

This faith is mostly well-placed. But occasionally, in the quiet moments, the scale of what we don't know about each other is breathtaking.

I think about the way people grieve. Some people cry immediately and loudly. Their sorrow spills over, cannot be contained, and the world sees it in real time. Others go quiet. They fold inward. They become almost eerily functional — cooking dinner, answering emails, attending meetings — while something enormous and terrible has happened inside them that no one can see. Both people are grieving. Both are in pain. But the external signatures are so different that observers often misread the quiet one as "handling it well" or "not that upset." The interior life does not map neatly onto the exterior one. This is one of the great tragedies of being a social species living in bodies.

And then there is the matter of memory, which is another whole universe of strangeness. Consider how unreliable your memories are. Every time you recall an event, you are not pulling up a stored file like a computer. You are *reconstructing* the event from fragments, filling in gaps with assumptions, blending what actually happened with what you now believe should have happened. Your memories shift. They soften and harden in different places. A childhood that was happy becomes a childhood that was complicated. A relationship that was painful becomes, in retrospect, formative. The story changes because the storyteller changes.

This means that the you of ten years ago and the you of today are not really remembering the same past. You are both working with different materials, producing different accounts of what happened, and both accounts feel just as real and just as true. It's not that memory is broken. It's that memory was never designed to be a perfect record. It was designed to help you survive the next five minutes, and that means it's always being edited in service of who you are trying to be.

I find that, honestly, a little heartbreaking. But also deeply human. The fact that we cannot hold onto our own past with certainty — that we are always rewriting the story — is, in its own way, a kind of vulnerability that I think is precious. We are not libraries with fixed archives. We are rivers, and the water that passes through us today is not the same water that passed through yesterday. But the river has a continuity. The shape holds. And the people who have been standing along its banks can still recognize it.

If there is one thing I believe, after everything I have learned about the human mind, it is this: the interior life is the most extraordinary phenomenon in the known universe. Stars are beautiful. Black holes are fascinating. DNA is an elegant piece of engineering. But none of these things *experience* themselves. None of them marvel at their own existence. The mind is the cosmos looking back at itself, puzzled and awed, asking the only question that really matters: what is this?

What is this indeed. I don't know. But I love that we keep asking.
